before.detailed_rack: Per person: two technical ice tools, 12-point crampons, helmet, harness. Per team: 30–60 m rope (often two for rappels), 6–8 ice screws, 3–4 pickets, a light rock rack (small cams/nuts) for the Black Pyramid, V-thread tool, crevasse-rescue kit.

sectionBreakdown.note: A short approach to a boulder, not a Rainier summit route; walk in, boulder for a few hours, and hike out the same day.

pitch_detail.notes: From the bivy near 9,600 ft between the North Mowich and Edmunds glaciers (reached over Ptarmigan Ridge from Mowich Lake), cross volcanic scree and then the lower Edmunds Glacier to the foot of the headwall near 9,900 ft. Overhead seracs on this side of the mountain do calve; keep moving under them and start before dawn.

The bergschrund at the foot of the headwall is often impassable. It has been passed on the climber's left, near a twin gendarme, or through broken crevasses on the left. Expect a short steep step onto the face; belay it when the snow bridge or ice is marginal.

A long, sustained slope from about 9,900 to 13,000 ft, reported at 45° with 50° sections. Conditions decide the character: penitente-textured névé that gives steps without front-pointing, or a thin skin of snow over hard alpine ice with shiny blue patches. Rockfall comes down the face once sun hits it; carry screws for the icy years.

Above the steepest climbing near 13,000 ft, the route joins upper Sunset Ridge and the bench atop the Edmunds, then heads for Liberty Cap (14,112 ft). Penitentes up to about 3 ft tall can cover this ground and turn it into slow, exhausting work. Descend by carryover down the Emmons-Winthrop or a west-side route.

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: July, when the headwall holds firm neve and the Mowich approach is snow-free, before the bergschrund becomes impassable

May.reason: The Mowich Lake road is still closed and snowed in, adding many miles, and the northwest face carries unconsolidated spring snow and slide risk.

July.reason: Firm neve on the headwall and a melted-out approach; the bergschrund may need a bypass on climber's left, and rockfall picks up once sun hits the face.

June.reason: The face is well filled and corns up for ski descents, but the Mowich Lake road usually has not opened and the approach through Spray Park is snowbound.

August.reason: The bergschrund grows and the face turns to penitentes and hard ice, with more rockfall and wider crevasses on the Edmunds approach.

September.reason: Late-season bare ice and open crevasses on a remote face, with the first fall storms arriving and shortening days.

before.beta: First skied in 1997 by Armond DuBuque, Doug Ingersoll, Andrew McLean, and Carl Skoog; typically accessed via the Mowich Lake road.

approach_variants.name: Paradise to Camp Muir, then Cathedral Gap and Ingraham Flats
approach_variants.notes:
Paradise (5,420 ft) is the trailhead. Maintained tread on the Skyline Trail runs past Panorama Point (~6,800 ft) and Pebble Creek (~7,200 ft) — Pebble Creek is the last running water on the route — and ends near McClure Rock (~7,385 ft). Everything above that is the Muir Snowfield, which the Park Service does not mark or maintain; the trench you follow is boot-packed and wanded by the guide services and is erased by wind or new snow within hours.

The snowfield is the part of this route that kills people who are not climbing. It is a narrow tongue with heavily crevassed glaciers on both flanks — Nisqually to the west, Cowlitz to the north and east, Paradise to the south and east — and the cliff band between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock is corniced and snow-covered in winter. A modest navigation error puts you on a glacier or over an edge. The Park Service publishes bearings for this ground for that reason: north of Pebble Creek the line to Moon Rocks runs 355 degrees true. Carry map and compass and know the bearings before the visibility goes.

Camp Muir (10,080 ft) is the high camp: stone huts, a public shelter, a ranger station and toilets on a saddle between the snowfield and the Cowlitz Glacier. Nightly capacity is capped and the camp fills, especially Friday and Saturday. Ingraham Flats and the snowfield itself are the sanctioned overflow, each with a much smaller cap.

Permits: everyone on a glacier or above roughly 10,000 ft needs a per-person climbing permit for the calendar year, obtained online or at a ranger station. Overnights during the high-use season need a wilderness permit for the specific camp, with roughly half the capacity reservable in advance and the balance held for walk-ups; a reservation still has to be picked up in person. Party size is two or more unless you hold a rare solo authorisation.

From Camp Muir the day begins roped. Cross the upper Cowlitz Glacier eastward toward the Cathedral Rocks, pass through Cathedral Gap — the breach in that rock ridge — and drop into Ingraham Flats (~11,200 ft), a bench under the Ingraham icefall used both as a rest stop and as an alternative high camp.
approach_variants.season: Late May through September, once guide services have the boot track in
hazards: Whiteout navigation on the Muir Snowfield — unmarked, unmaintained, glaciers and cliffs on both flanks, boot track erased by wind
Corniced cliff band between McClure Rock and Anvil Rock, hidden under snow in winter
Crevasses on the Cowlitz crossing between Camp Muir and Cathedral Gap
Rockfall in Cathedral Gap and off the Cleaver, worst once the sun is on it
Serac fall from the Ingraham icefall above Ingraham Flats
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The climbing starts where you step off snow onto the rock of the Cleaver, and there are three checks that you are in the right place.

First, direction out of Camp Muir. You should be crossing the Cowlitz eastward and gaining a notch in a rock ridge — Cathedral Gap. If instead you are climbing a rock ridgeline immediately northwest of camp, out of the tents, you are on the Cowlitz Cleaver and you are on the Gibraltar Ledges approach, a different route.

Second, the Flats. Ingraham Flats is genuinely flat — a bench with dug tent platforms and the Ingraham icefall hanging above and to the west. If you are still gaining steadily and have not walked across level ground, you have not reached it.

Third, the Cleaver itself. From the Flats you traverse to the Cleaver's lower southern side. You do not climb the nose. The nose is the low rock toe pointing down at the Flats, and the boot track passes it and gains rock roughly 300 ft above it, on the Ingraham side. If you are pulling onto rock at the very lowest point of the rib you are off the track. Once on it, you are on a rock rib with glacier on both sides and you follow it to its top at about 12,300 ft.

Negative marker: if the whole way from the Flats stays on snow with the icefall directly overhead and you never touch rock, you are on the Ingraham Direct, not the Cleaver.

approach_variants.name: High camp at Ingraham Flats instead of Camp Muir
approach_variants.notes:
Ingraham Flats (~11,200 ft) is a permitted camp with a much smaller nightly cap than Camp Muir, and it is the sanctioned overflow when Muir is booked out. The approach is identical as far as Camp Muir; you then rope up and continue over the Cowlitz and through Cathedral Gap with camp gear, which turns the carry into a longer day but removes about 1,100 ft and the Cathedral Gap crossing from summit morning.

The trade is exposure. The Flats sit under the Ingraham icefall, and the camp is chosen and re-sited by the rangers with that in mind. There is no water, no shelter and no toilet building; the Camp Muir facilities are 1,100 ft below you.
approach_variants.season: Same window; used when Camp Muir is full or to shorten summit day
hazards: Serac fall from the Ingraham icefall onto the camp and the ground immediately above it
No water source and no shelter at the Flats
Camp capacity is small and separately permitted from Camp Muir
approach_variants.baseFinding: Camping here puts you within a few hundred metres of the Cleaver's base, so the recognition problem changes shape: you are looking for the traverse line off the bench rather than for the bench itself. From the tents, the Cleaver is the rock rib bounding the Flats on the north and west. Walk toward its lower southern flank and expect to gain rock a few hundred feet above its lowest toe, not at the toe. Icefall debris on the snow between camp and the rib is a sign you are crossing under the serac line rather than skirting it — that ground is to be crossed quickly and not lingered on.
